Content: So is the beef from the representative country or are you just comparing cooking styles?  If the beef is from the country then with the Australian one is from the Angus cow? Which region of Australia is it from? Is it grass fed? Because all these and more can play an important factor. For example beef from northern Western Australia texture and taste are vastly different to southern Western Australia. The north is arid country and the cattle roam large areas feeding on what they can find compared to lush green paddocks of the south. Paddock fed which is most Australian cattle including dairy cows has different flavour and texture then compared to USA lot fed on corn meal. Angus is one of Australia’s prime meat cattle compared to say a Holstein which is primarily a dairy cow.  I would willing put an Angus grass fed steak up against most other beef especially the USA. Most Aussies generally don’t do a surf and turf either, that’s normally special occasions, normally a pepper gravy, mushroom gravy, or even a blue cheese sauce whatever your preference is, is served with a steak.

Author: @giannigrassi1047
Content:
As an Italian From Firenze where bistecca alla fiorentina comes from I would like to explain:
The steak must be four finger height otherwise it's a simple chop, the only way to cook it is rare and the charcoal must be on a very high temperature so we get the crost on the outside and it seals the juices in the inside. Of course we add the seasoning but after the bistecca is cooked and it's not just salt. First of all we add the tuscan extra virgin olive oil which has a strong and intense flavour and little bit spicy very different than any other oil (even from Italy) , then coarse salt and black pepper. There you have got the real Bistecca.

Author: @xarz3
Content:
I'm italian and I've never seen anybody with the guts of serving fiorentina with a salad on top and in a plain ceramic plate that doesn’t keep it hot.

How can you judge it like that?

Fiorentina must be eaten hot, such that often it's served on cast iron skillets, or at most on a wooden board.

You put something on top cold like a salad, you ruined it. Not to mention that oil and garlic sauce... that's not how it's done. 

The proper way is take the meat hot from the hot serving plate and put a few pieces into your plate. Then you put salt, pepper if you like, and pour few drips of high quality raw olive oil directly from the bottle on top of the hot meat and eat right away. Then you take the next piece and repeat.

You don't do rosemary, garlic, zest sauces. You don't put salad on top of it and you dont serve it cold like that.

Author: @jinkim145
Content:
One of the most common mistakes foreigners make when eating Korean BBQ is not eating everything in one bite. The reason we wrap meat in lettuce isn’t just for health—it’s also so the whole wrap can be eaten in a single bite.

In the West, people are used to foods like hamburgers or tacos, which you usually bite into. But with Korean BBQ, the key is to pop the entire wrap into your mouth at once. That way, your hands don’t get messy.

If you try to bite into it, the juices from the meat, kimchi, or sauce inside the lettuce can spill out and make things messy.

Who told you that was *the* Australian version of steak and how it's supposed to be done?    You were right about the medium rare... but that was about it.   Unfortunately, you made a point of saying you weren't going to do anything special, offered very little info other than it was a thick steak, and then unsurprisingly arrived at it being nothing special.   Not particularly Australian.   

Just to start,  if you sourced that there in the states, it either wasn't an Australian steak (which matters a lot) or it had been frozen for transport at some point.  In either case, you were off track already.  Bone-in ribeye, while not uncommon, isn't in the top 3 most popular cuts in Australia. Then there's the unmentioned fact that Australia is particularly noted for wagyu - to the extent that it's exported to Japan.     So while you're doing all you can to do right by every other steak and country, at the very least, why not a proper high country, grass-fed, wagyu cut for Australia?  

Part of the issue with this is that there really isn't a stock standard, uniquely Australian way to serve a steak.  Aussies' particular skill is in welcoming in ideas from all over, which means you see plenty of chimichurri, reductions, mushroom duxelles, garlic butter, coffee rubs and just about every other possibility.   But since none of that is exclusively Australian and y'all weren't into digging deeper, Australia seems to have been put out there as the default "plain steak" eaters.    But it's not.   Not really.   No more so than in Texas, for instance, which also has its share of "steak is fine by itself" diners.  (used to cook there)    

Now, if you were serving up that grass-fed wagyu with a 6-7 MB score (instead of a stock standard Costco ribeye), then "plain is good enough" might have actually been true.

I'm from beef country in the US, with beef producers in the family.  And I've been in Australia for a good while.  The beef doesn't taste the same.   A real steak fiend would start with a lot of info about the steak itself and wouldn't necessarily do nothing to a steak other than chuck it on the fire with a thick coat of salt on it.   (ps, they also don't put shrimp on the barbie down here.   Nothing says you don't know Australia more than using shrimp and barbie in the same commentary, :))    Aussies eat prawns. 

Anyway, every other place got the full treatment and it all looked delicious, from guac to galbi, but I do think Aussie got the scraps when it came to this cook-off.    Write me some time if you ever would like to talk about things Australia does do differently ..... for instance, it has a slew of delicious native spices and herbs not found anywhere else that have been in use for somewhere around 40,000 years.   We enjoy Tasmanian Mountain Pepperberry and roast espresso coffee as our preferred steak seasoning... and lemon myrtle with "chicken salt" on our wings!

Author: @knirfien2091
Content:
I have had Bistecca alla Florentina several times, and I have never had it served like this. 
There is always salt or spiced salt on the table so you can add the amount that you like. And normally it gets basted with an infused olive oil, or oil/butter mixture during cooking, i've never seen in drowned in oil during plating.

Also, next time try our shitty Dutch steak: which would generally be a top sirloin filet (but you can substitute with tenderloin filet, chuck tender or eye of round for different prize categories), often a cut is used from a young cow or sometimes even veal, but this is not a must. It is pan fried in butter and served almost drowning in butter sauce.

Salt the steak. Melt 50 grams of butter over a pan on medium heat, add white onion rings and cook until golden, remove the onion and set aside. Add another 100 grams of butter to the pan, increase heat to high, add the filet when butter is ready. Cook steak until medium rare, remove steak and let rest. Add a little bit of hot water to the butter, and reduce on low heat to a nice butter sauce.
Serve the steak with the onions, reduced butter sauce, freshly cracked black pepper, a salad and bread (or potatoes). As simple, boring and unhealthy as it can get...

Author: @LAghemo
Content:
I'm an Italian and a long time Guga follower, I love to learn recepies and techniques from everywhere, although I incredibly love Italian cooking, and I enjoy using some "fusion" when I cook. But I feel the urge of a small clarification here.
Italian cooking is simpler and more delicate than other part of the world. Even French cooking (that I adore btw) and that might be considered "near" to Italian, is much more "fat" and elaborate than Italian one. Example: everyone think we use a lot of garlic in tomato sauce, but we don't! We put a clove in the olive oil while is heating and then take it out before eating! We tend to eat things "as they are", mixed in different way to acheive different flavours, but with less seasoning than the rest of the world. 
So here comes the problem with Italians cooking meat: we are not used to all the seasoning that is used in the other countries. I can say myself that, learning from the rest of the world how to cook steaks, I started seasoning mine a couple of hours before cooking. And now I stopped doing it, because I like to taste the meat as it is, not "altered" by all the seasoning. Salt? Later. Pepper? Later but maybe not. Garlic powder... are you kidding me? That's also the reason why we tend to eat meat a bit more rare, to taste its real flavour.
So I think that there's no absolute but this is a matter of background and habits. I think I can say that for most italians a steak like the Korean one, that you considered the best, would be maybe great for one or two small pieces, but then it would be "too much", maybe even nauseating for someone. Basically... I think that this video might be good for people with Americans food habits, but not for everyone. Not for Italians for sure.
But... wait a moment... isn't italian kitchen considerer one of the best in the world? And healthier?
Meditate on this thou shall.
Oh! BTW: "Entrecote" sauce is French, not English! The word itself "entrecôte" is in french language, and it is a "secret" receipe from the restaurant "Relais de l'entrecôte" born in Paris. Like "French fries".

Author: @moonjoun1
Content:
I usually recommend going to a specialty restaurant for marinated short ribs (yangnyeom-galbi) rather than trying to make them at home. It’s not an easy dish to get right, mainly because making the sauce correctly is very difficult. Using the juice from fruits like apples or Korean pears instead of just sugar doesn't just add sweetness—it also helps to tenderize the meat.
Once the sauce is made, marinating the meat elevates its flavor and texture.
The real challenge, however, is the grilling process. Unlike a typical steak, the window for perfectly cooked galbi is very short. It's easy to burn it. Achieving that beautiful golden-brown color requires a lot of experience and effort (I'm 38, and I still mess it up sometimes!).
Also, while there are many dishes you can make with ribs, I prefer using pork for grilled marinated ribs and beef for galbi-jjim (braised beef short ribs). I actually think foreigners might prefer galbi-jjim.

Author: @arsoncrafts136
Content:
Tataki-gyu probably would have been a better choice than teppan-yaki.  If you want something that is really interesting and stands out from normal steak, that will work much better than just regular Japanese steak you have had before.

Tataki-gyu is beef tenderloin - even with wagyu, it won’t be too fatty and the texture is amazing.

Generous salt and pepper, then you hit it with a blowtorch as hot as possibly, getting an aggressive crust and every level of flavor and texture from almost burned to raw.

Then you plunge it into ice water to stop the cooking process - they very aggressive crust will stop the water from really washing away a lot of flavor.

Then you slice it very thin - sushi style (thinner than most sashimi).

This is served with momiji-oroshi. Momiji-oroshi is daikon , peeled and cut in half - three holes are poked in the daikon with a chopstick and Japanese chili peppers are inserted, then the daikon is grated on an oroshigane, a Japanese style grater.  

Along with the momiji-oroshi you serve with sliced green onion and ponzu (a yuzu-vinegar-shoyu sauce).

It’s incredible, the sauce and grated daikon really cut through the fat with a little bit of spice kick (togarashi peppers are not very hot at all)

It’s one of my absolute favorites.

Content:

Author: @ptdraks
Content:
Why on earth did you pick Bife à Cerveja to represent Portugal? That’s not even a common dish here. If you want something truly Portuguese, go with Bife à Café—now that’s the classic. It’s made with two shots of espresso, heavy cream, mustard, garlic, and poured over a steak like it’s royalty. Sure, it’s not your traditional beef dish, but it’s ours. Rich, bold, and unapologetically Portuguese.

You could choose this one’s;


Bife à Café	Steak with a bold coffee-based sauce.	Espresso, cream, mustard, garlic	

Bife à Portuguesa	The quintessential Portuguese steak, often topped with a fried egg. Garlic, wine, butter, fried egg, fries A thin steak served with fries, rice, and a fried egg. Garlic marinade, white wine, bay leaf	

Prego no Pão	A steak sandwich served in soft bread, often with mustard or piri-piri. Sirloin steak, garlic, mustard, olive oil	

Prego no Prato	Similar to Bitoque but served on a plate with sides  Steak, rice, fries, salad, egg	

Bife com Presunto	Steak topped with crispy ham and a savory sauce. Ham, mustard, garlic, white wine	

Bife com Molho de Vinho  Steak in a rich red wine sauce. Red wine, garlic, butter, tomato paste	

Bife à Marrare	A Lisbon classic with a creamy mushroom sauce. Mushrooms, cream, garlic, butter

Next time Search and ask to a Native Portuguese what is the most common steak dish and I am certain is not Bife à cerveja … and not acavalo hahah only a few will understand (bife a cavalo)😅

Author: @ozidanni
Content:
Australian here. I'm glad that was nice, but it wasn't an Aussie steak mates. Haha. I've never seen a tomohawk cut here. I've never seasoned with salt and pepper, and I've never bbq'd a prawn. Haha. 

Usually steak here is just simply about the quality of the meat, and the cut. If bbq'd it'll usually be a flat plate cleaned with beer (not open rack like that.). Author: @faampie
Content:
I'm from South Africa, and we LOVE meat. Between me and my wife we go through 1-1.5kg (2.2-3.3lbs) of meat every dinner. 
Most of our meals are cooked over a open fire with hot coals (wood, not charcoal). It is called a "braai" and is a South African tradition.
I can't say that we have a specific steak or sauce that can be called a national dish. It is sort of a personal choice. BUT, those choices get very personal. You get guys that only use gas, only use charcoal or only use wood. And they normally don't even talk to each other. Then there is the cooking styles (flames, coals, skillet, etc), should the meat be marinated , basted, only spiced, etc. We can't even agree on what wood should be used.  You can start a civil war by arguing about the way a man braai in SA. 
But thanks to a guy called Guga I learned about garlic and onion powder. So now my favorite way to do a steak is to marinade my steak for a few hours in a mix of Worcestersauce with garlic and onion powder (and a few other secret ingredients). Then it is flame grilled on a wood fire.

Author: @rudycory1721
Content:
22:00 so in here there are some minor misunderstandongs about how you server a Fiorentina, first thing first the seasoning: yes we Italian often do not season our meat with salt... *While it's on the grill. When it gets a nice crust, and it's still hot, THEN you can had your salt and pepper to your liking!
because it is popular belief in Italy that salt right before cooking could cause the meat to be tougher (I know it sounds dumb but it is what it is) and also, people in a grill out are often advised to had salt or pepper if they feel like it's leaking.
Second thing, now I'm not sure if that's the authentic way of making it but in some restaurants also sever it on a hot plate, so if it's not on your liking you can get at your right temperature.
Overall, this is just a minor criticism, not offending anyone just what to leave a constructive explanation to clear out some misinformations. Italian meat grilling, like all forms of social gatherings, it's about conviviality (you don't want to give your friends a unsalty slab of tough meat)
Not serving the British steak with either a peppercorn or a beef dripping sauce was criminal.

Author: @davidoliveira7184
Content:
Oi Guga - Portuguese here:
Thanks for bringing attention to Portuguese cuisine in general!

But you’re mixing up "bitoque" [everyday utility food, with default egg], with "bife à cerveja" [no egg, and a very niche Portuguese big-city brasserie only thing]. 
All of which, no one in Portugal would ever put on a “national team of dishes” for international competition.

For a dream team like that, look into the original “7 Maravilhas da Gastronomia Portuguesa”, with additional "sweet" and "contemporary" spin-offs. 
(perhaps all these deserve their own video for international audiences 😉).

As for steaks, the only dish you could genuinely call something like “Portuguese steak” would be definitely “Posta”, namely “Posta à Mirandesa” (actually officially *DOP* certified, like a fine wine or cheese). Or, “Posta” from the town of Arouca, all made from very special "primordial" cows.

PS: Fun fact -- the "Arouca" town name is said - by some (not proven) - to come from "Auroch", the wild ancestor of today's domesticated cows.

Author: @TheAratine
Content:
In Norway we have a traditional dish called Sosekjøtt. It's basically a dish made out of necessity where you sear off cubed pieces of beef(somewhat large pieces) coated with salt, pepper and flour. Then you add it to beef stock, add some translucent-cooked yellow onions and use corn flour to thicken. It's a beef and brown gravy stew where you slow-cook the beef in the gravy itself. Usually served with boiled potatoes but I like mashed as a base for it.
Reason behind this method was to make make something tasty and tender out of cheaper, tougher cuts of beef.

Content:
As an Italian:
- "Bistecca alla Fiorentina" is just a Tuscan thing – not all of Italy. It’s usually salted before or after grilling, but yes, a few people eat it even without salt… basically raw – almost like the cow is still chewing grass. 😂
- More common is "tagliata di manzo" – pre-salted, usually medium/medium-rare unless you ask, served with arugula & Parmigiano.
- At home we grill "grigliata mista" (mixed grill) with salsiccia (sausages), costine (ribs), braciole (pork chops), seasoned with salt, rosemary, black pepper, but also often garlic, sage, extra virgin olive oil, lemon, bay leaves, chili, oregano, thyme or parsley – it depends on the region.

👉 Maybe your teacher was the same guy who eats pasta not “al dente” (“to the tooth”), but “al sasso” (“like a rock”). 😉

That said florentine steak is delicious and i suggest everyone to tray it (just in tuscany or tuscan places with imported meat and trained cooks), but it's far from being the best steak in the world. i am no chauvinist or food snob and i love other cultures and acknowledge their superiority when due. but you should also stop butchering my own culture

Author: @collinsmcrae
Content:
The reason that well done beef became the preference south of the US border, is the same reason that well done pork and chicken are the preference here. It's a matter of food safety.

These days, most countries In  Central and SA can certainly store and distribute beef that can safely be cooked to rare or medium rare, but that's a recent development in many countries, and some aren't quite there in the poorest of communities.

When soemthing is done one way for safety for long enough, it can actually become a taste preference. For instance, when it comes to most pork products, the current regulations are pretty much on par with beef, yet I flat out prefer medium to medium-well pork. I'm a rare steak guy, but even though safe temps have gone up for chicken and pork, I still prefer them as if that weren't the case.

Author: @jasonconley5744
Content:
Guga, here are a few more famous steak dishes from other countries:

1. Kitfo (Ethiopia) - this is similar to tartare, so the kids might not like it.
2. Buuz/Huushuur (Mongolia) - whole muscle cuts, thin dough casing, good luck.
3. Arayes (Lebanon) - finished in a pita, then grilled.
4. Tasso (Haiti) - marinated, flash fried, right up your alley.
5. Bò Lúc Lạc ("Shaking Beef," Vietnam) - more wok work.
6. Ropa Vieja (Cuba) - the flank is shredded at the end, but the sauce is light.
7. Lomo Saltado (Peru) - sirloin holds up the bold seasonings.

I avoided recommending sauce-heavy, but famous, pasta-steak dishes like goulash and stroganoff. They don’t let the flavor of the steak shine through.

Author: @Dr_V
Content:
If you ever get to Romania you'll hear about 2 types of steak that are in fact cooked exactly the same, the only difference being the cut of meat: "biftec" (which funnily enough comes from the English "beef steak" written phonetically in Romanian) means T-bone and "antricot" (from the French "entrecôte") meaning rib-eye. 
To prepare the meat season it on both sides with plenty of salt but just a pinch of pepper (say about half what you'd normally use), than put it in the fridge for 24 hours at 5C (~40F) and let it slowly reach room temperature before cooking. 
Cooking is done on a charcoal grill pretty much the same as your regular technique but going for medium, not medium-rare. 
An authentic and popular side-dish would be rosemary baked potatoes: wedged or quartered, seasoned with salt, pepper, sweet paprika, chopped rosemary and crushed garlic, baked in olive oil at medium heat for 30-40 minutes.

Let me explain how I have eaten steaks in the UK for 40+ years.. 
Sirloin steak.  Season with Salt and pepper ONLY!
Steak sauce is a pepper sauce and it is NOT applied directly to the steak.  It is eaten with the steak.
Serve with Mashed potatoes, vegetables of Carrots and Peas.  Sauce applied to the vegetables and beside the steak.

Some people may apply the sauce to the steak.. But it should not be on the steak until you are ready to eat it.  Its a side sauce and not a Marinade.

Author: @AlyxiSistahTweaky25
Content:
Living in SE Asia, thanks to the large expat communities in places like Bangkok and Singapore, we have a ton of imported meats. Various grades of picanha from Brazil, USA, Japan (and real Kobe if you want to spend the money at either of the two "official" places that serve it), Australia beef, NZ, Argentina, and I have even seen Mexico and China. And of course more local sources like Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam. All at various price points.  Being on a budget, I have limited myself to the more affordable sources and grades.  Being in Thailand now, the easiest way to get high-grade ribeye is of course Thai beef.  So a Thai "waygu" A4 would be around the same cost as USDA Choice....not really a fair comp.  But overall, the best I have had here was a one inch thick Australian grass fed MB7, GP/S/P, sous vide to 125ºF, short rest, ghee in the cast iron hot AF, one minute each side to sear and baste with rosemary butter.  I splurged a bit.  And the best I have ever had anywhere was at a steakhouse in New Jersey, a 60 day dry aged sirloin, even though ribeye or picanha is usually my preferred cut. That was 20+ years ago, so my memory may be playing tricks on me.

I think a proper comparison would be using the locally produced beef for each country's preferred preparation. 
Alternately, you could use the same cut and preparation using each country's beef.  Picanhas from around the world!

Content: That last steak, unfortunately, has very little to do with England. The sauce is a Cafe de Paris sauce, and comes from the Entrecôte restaurant that started in Geneva, Switzerland. The recipe for the gourmet butter sauce the restaurants use is secret, and I believe only known to the families that own the restaurants (there are imitations of course), and is more liquidy and buttery than the one in the vid.
